newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche seeks exit from Horlick row - source.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche seeks exit from Horlick row - source.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG is determined not to be dragged any further into the drama over fund manager Nicola Horlick's departure from its British asset management arm MGAM, banking sources said on Monday.

"The press have had their field day and that's an end of it," said one source close to events, referring to the media coverage of Horlick's tale of what she says was constructive dismissal by the German bank.

Press officials at Deutsche Bank's Frankfurt headquarters, who were confronted by a crusading Horlick on Friday literally on their doorstep, referred inquiries on the case, the second major scandal to hit the bank in months, to London.

Last September Deutsche was hit by a probe into alleged mismanagement of funds by MGAM fund manager Peter Young -- a scandal which cost the bank 200 million pounds ($332 million) compensation and caused heads to roll at MGAM.

Horlick, once Morgan Grenfell Asset Management's top pension fund manager, resigned her position last Thursday in a blaze of publicity, having been suspended amid allegations that she tried to lure a team of colleagues to another bank.
Although her departure is not directly linked to the Young affair, Horlick says the furore has its roots in the discontent sparked by the management reshuffle after Young's dismissal.

The loquacious 35-year-old, who denies the charges against her and wants compensation or reinstatement, dragged Deutsche directly into the fray on Friday when she made a solo trip to Frankfurt to seek an audience with its management board.
"She may be a highly capable fund manager and earn more than a Deutsche Bank board member, but that doesn't mean anyone here would know her," said a second banking source.

Horlick did manage to meet a senior legal officer of the bank and a top personnel executive and has expressed interest in pursuing those talks. But Deutsche was quick to stress that London would be the chief venue for any future talks.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the bank's British investment banking arm, is leading a probe into Horlick's situation, which has focused on interviewing former colleagues of the woman who, with five children, was dubbed the "Superwoman" of the City.
"We did not take the initiative to bring the talks to Frankfurt, that came from Ms Horlick herself," said the legal official who spoke with Horlick on Friday.

"We still consider it appropriate that the focus of the investigations is in London. All the experts are there and we would not consider it appropriate to take matters into our hands," he told Reuters, asking not to be identified.

Analysts have played down the impact of the recent double blow to the image of Europe's largest bank, noting that they showed problems were inevitable as it pursued a ferocious expansion in a highly competitive market.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was this week preparing an intensive campaign to shore up its 18 billion pound British pension fund business, of which Horlick managed about a fifth.
On Monday, Britain's Norfolk County Council said it was keeping its pension fund contract with MGAM under review.

Deutsche spared no expense hiring specialists and buying computerised trading equipment in an expansion launched in 1994 at Morgan Grenfell, which it bought in 1989. Horlick herself was hired in from Mercury Asset Management in 1990.
Meanwhile, Horlick's lawyer said on Monday that his client was still seeking an amicable settlement with her former employers but said she would also consider legal action.
"This could go on for months ... years," said one banking source in Frankfurt.
